 Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is promising swift action following voters' approval of Amendment 3, setting a Jan. 1 deadline for implementing property tax relief while preparing measures to prevent local governments from offsetting lost revenue with new fees. 
 LAKE WALES, Fla. — Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is promising to deliver property tax relief within weeks, announcing plans for a special legislative session to implement Amendment 3 following its approval by voters Tuesday.
 "That has to be done by January 1st, and we will do it by January 1st," DeSantis declared Wednesday during an appearance at Polk State College.
 The governor said he will work with legislative leaders to schedule the session before leaving office in January.
 Tax relief — but no replacement fees 
 Amendment 3 provides property tax relief for qualifying homesteaded properties while preserving school district property taxes.
 DeSantis has warned that local governments must not undermine the tax cuts by replacing lost property tax revenue with higher fees or other charges.
 "It's not going to be a tax shift. It's going to be a reduction," DeSantis said during earlier post-election remarks.
 He wants lawmakers to establish taxpayer protections that would limit attempts to circumvent the amendment.
 What about police, fire and other services? 
 The governor also plans to work with lawmakers on financial assistance for local governments facing reduced property tax collections.
 He has proposed a state grant program to help communities, particularly rural counties with smaller tax bases, maintain essential services such as sheriff's departments.
 DeSantis said Florida has sufficient resources to manage the transition.
 "Everything's gonna be fine. We're gonna work it out. We've got a lot of resources," he said Wednesday.
 Deadline approaching 
 The governor has not announced a date for the special session, saying legislative leaders will help determine the schedule.
 The implementing legislation must be completed before the amendment's Jan. 1 effective date.
 For Florida homeowners, the promise is significant: Property tax relief is coming. But lawmakers now face a tight deadline to determine how the cuts will work — and how local governments will continue paying for essential services.
